## Description

The first immortal human cell line (1951, from Henrietta Lacks' cervical adenocarcinoma). Epithelial
and polygonal (~40 µm spread, ~2600 µm³). It does not stop dividing when the dish fills (it piles
up) and has a high aerobic glycolysis: it turns much glucose into lactate (Warburg effect), which
acidifies the medium.

## In the simulation

<!-- GENERATED:presence -->
Drops: not seeded in the default drops (inoculate it from the Catalogue).
<!-- /GENERATED -->

An adherent [animal cell](../../mechanics/animal-cells.md) **without contact inhibition of proliferation**, with
little migration and a Warburg lactate yield of ~1.5–2 per glucose. Validated: doubling time and the
lactate/glucose ratio.

## Literature

- Puck T.T., Marcus P.I., Cieciura S.J. (1956) J. Exp. Med. 103: 273 (HeLa S3 generation ~20 h at
  37 °C).
- Jain M. et al. (2012) Metabolite profiling identifies a key role for glycine in rapid cancer cell
  proliferation. Science 336: 1040–1044 (NCI-60 glucose, glutamine and lactate fluxes).
- Alberts B. et al. *Molecular Biology of the Cell*, 6th ed., fig. 17-4 (S 8 h, G2 4 h, M 1 h of a typical human cell).
- Carruthers A. (1990) Facilitated diffusion of glucose. Physiol. Rev. 70: 1135–1176 (GLUT1 Km ~1–3 mM).

## Not implemented yet

- Cells do not really pile up in 3D (the view is a plane).
- No clonogenic assay or dose–response of drugs on eukaryotes.
- No phase-contrast lens yet: cultures are seen in bright field (roadmap C).
- Not supported in the well-mixed culture.

## Unique and shared mechanics

The Warburg effect and the lack of contact inhibition distinguish it from the fibroblasts; shares the
[animal-cell machinery](../../mechanics/animal-cells.md).
